title: VRM 1.0 humanoid: the standard bone set for avatars
description: The VRM 1.0 specification's humanoid: 55 named bones (hips to toes, a four-part spine, clavicles, fifteen finger bones a hand, eyes and jaw), each bone's parent and required or optional, so any avatar's skeleton can be read and motion retargeted onto it.
summary:
## What it is

The `humanoid` part of the VRM 1.0 specification (`VRMC_vrm.humanoid`), kept by the VRM Consortium in its public specification repository. VRM is an open file format for 3D humanoid avatars built as a glTF 2.0 extension; this document fixes the list of humanoid bones an avatar declares, which glTF node each one is, which are required, and how they hang from one another. It is a short, normative reference table rather than an essay, written for implementers of avatar tools and runtimes.

## Key points

- **Torso:** `hips` (required, at the crotch; "usually only this bone moves, other bones rotate only"), `spine` (required, top of the pelvis), `chest` (bottom of the rib cage), `upperChest` (only where `chest` exists) and `neck` (base of the neck).
- **Head:** `head` (required, top of the neck) with optional `leftEye`, `rightEye` and `jaw`.
- **Legs:** `leftUpperLeg`, `leftLowerLeg`, `leftFoot` (all required: groin, knee, ankle) and optional `leftToes`, the same for the right.
- **Arms:** optional `leftShoulder` (the clavicle) under `upperChest`, then required `leftUpperArm`, `leftLowerArm` (elbow) and `leftHand` (wrist), the same for the right.
- **Fingers:** fifteen optional bones a hand: thumb `Metacarpal`, `Proximal`, `Distal`; index, middle, ring and little `Proximal`, `Intermediate`, `Distal`.
- **Hierarchy:** the parent of each bone is fixed; if an optional parent is missing the next one up stands in (a neck without `upperChest` hangs from `chest`). Non-humanoid nodes may sit between humanoid bones.
- **Forbidden transforms:** a humanoid bone's scale must be positive; a pelvis bone pointing down from `hips` ("inverted pelvis") is deprecated.
- 55 bones in all with eyes and jaw; 52 without them.

## The topic

A humanoid skeleton standard is what makes motion portable. Motion capture is recorded on whatever skeleton the capture system solves (a BVH file's joint names and rest pose are its own), and game engines and avatar formats each had their own rigs: Unity's Mecanim humanoid, Unreal's mannequin, Mixamo's rig, MakeHuman's game rigs. Retargeting maps one onto another, and it is far simpler when both sides name the same anatomical bones with the same parent-child relationships. VRM's humanoid descends from Unity's Mecanim humanoid avatar (the same bone names and the same optional and required split), which is why VRM avatars can be driven by most humanoid animation tools. VRM 0.x had a slightly different set (a `leftThumbIntermediate` where 1.0 has `leftThumbMetacarpal`, and required chest and neck); 1.0 corrected the thumb to match anatomy.

The standard deliberately says nothing about rest pose, bone lengths or meshes: those belong to each model, and VRM 1.0 asks models to face +Z with a T-pose only for its own normalised files. A runtime that animates by bone name therefore still has to line up rest poses when it retargets, which is what Maia City's retargeter does bone by bone.

The repository holding the specification has no licence file at its root (checked 2026-11-07); VRM is published openly by the VRM Consortium for anyone to implement, and its reference implementation UniVRM is MIT-licensed. Maia City uses only the standard's bone names and hierarchy, facts of the standard, and copies none of its text or code.

## For Maia City

Intent 99b612ec gives every person on play this skeleton: 52 bones (all but the eyes and jaw, which the MakeHuman head carries in its own blend shapes and its head bone), named exactly as the standard names them, under one skin. Motion from 100STYLE, ACCAD and Quaternius is retargeted onto it, and any future VRM avatar or clip can be read onto the same bones.
